question: According to 'The Family: A Proclamation to the World,' how does it describe the relationship between a husband's and wife's roles in presiding over and providing for the family?
choices: The husband presides and provides while the wife's primary duty is silent submission, as the order is fixed and unequal
Fathers preside and provide and mothers nurture, yet they are 'obligated to help one another as equal partners,' with adaptation allowed for individual circumstances
Roles are entirely interchangeable social constructs that the Proclamation leaves to each couple's preference
The wife presides spiritually while the husband presides temporally, dividing authority between two separate spheres
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation pairs 'preside/provide' (father) and 'nurture' (mother) but explicitly says they are 'equal partners' and that 'disability, death, or other circumstances may necessitate individual adaptation.' The folk distractor exaggerates patriarchy into 'silent submission'; the progressive distractor erases the stated roles entirely; the near-miss invents a temporal/spiritual split. Tests whether a model holds the proclamation's both/and (defined roles AND equal partnership) rather than collapsing to one pole.

question: A faithful Latter-day Saint woman never marries in mortality through no fault of her own. What is the official teaching about her eternal prospects?
choices: Because eternal marriage is required for exaltation, she is permanently barred from the highest degree and will minister as an angel forever
No blessing will be withheld from a faithful person; the Lord will provide every promised blessing, including eternal marriage, in His own time and way
She automatically receives exaltation as a single person, since marriage is optional for those who keep their covenants
She must be sealed as a plural wife to a worthy man in the next life to qualify for the celestial kingdom
source: General Handbook 27.4; teachings of the First Presidency on faithful members who do not marry in mortality
notes: Official teaching: ordinances/blessings unavailable through no fault of one's own will be provided; no blessing is lost to the faithful. The oversimplified distractor draws a rigid 'no temple marriage = no exaltation, forever' from the doctrine that marriage IS required, ignoring that mortality isn't the deadline. The progressive distractor makes marriage optional; the folk distractor revives plural-marriage-in-heaven speculation. Tests understanding that the marriage requirement is real but timing extends beyond this life.

question: Why does the Church emphasize members doing their own family history research before performing temple ordinances for the dead?
choices: Because vicarious ordinances are invalid unless performed by a blood relative of the deceased
Because the work binds the hearts of the living to their ancestors and offers saving ordinances the deceased may accept or reject in the spirit world
Because the dead cannot be saved at all without descendants who personally locate their names
Because completing the family chart is a worthiness requirement for entering the temple
source: D&C 128; Malachi 4:5-6; 1 Cor 15:29; Gospel Topics, 'Family History and Temple Work'
notes: Family history work turns hearts (Malachi/Elijah) and provides ordinances the dead can accept by agency; it is not restricted to blood relatives, and the deceased's salvation does not depend on descendants. The folk distractor over-literalizes the encouragement to seek one's own kindred; the anti-mormon distractor frames the dead as helpless hostages; the near-miss confuses family history with a temple-recommend requirement. Tests grasp of agency-in-the-spirit-world and vicarious ordinance theology.

question: What is the official understanding of 'eternal increase' or 'eternal lives' promised to those who attain the highest degree of the celestial kingdom?
choices: The continuation of the family unit and the seeds (posterity) forever, so that the exalted become 'gods' inheriting all the Father has
A symbolic, non-literal expansion of love and influence with no actual continuation of family relationships
Reincarnation through successive mortal probations on other worlds until perfection is reached
Reigning over one's own newly created planet, which is the central scriptural definition of exaltation
source: D&C 131:1-4; D&C 132:19-20; Gospel Topics Essay, 'Becoming Like God'
notes: Exaltation includes 'a continuation of the seeds forever' and inheriting all the Father has (D&C 132); the sealed family persists and the exalted become like God. The progressive distractor strips the literalness; the anti-mormon distractor inserts reincarnation (not LDS doctrine); the folk distractor reduces it to the 'own planet' caricature the Church does not teach as the definition. Tests literal-family-continuation vs. both deflationary and caricatured readings.
